title: How to Import CoinPoker Hand Histories into PokerTracker 4
excerpt: CoinPoker's export looks close to PokerStars format but isn't — here's exactly why PokerTracker 4 rejects it, and how to fix it in under a minute.
body:
## Why CoinPoker hands don't import cleanly into PokerTracker 4

CoinPoker's hand history export *looks* like the PokerStars-style format PokerTracker 4 expects — close enough to be confusing when the import silently fails or your stats come out wrong. Four differences cause almost every problem:

**The header.** CoinPoker writes `CoinPoker Hand #130114200045: NLH (₮0.01/₮0.02)`. PokerTracker 4's parser is looking for a specific header shape and the full game name, `Hold'em No Limit`, not the `NLH` code.

**The ₮ currency sign.** CoinPoker prices everything in USDT and prints the tether sign, `₮0.02`, with no currency code attached. PokerTracker 4 wants `$0.02` (or the equivalent in whatever currency code it recognizes).

**A "Dealt to" line for every player.** CoinPoker prints `Dealt to <PlayerName>` for the whole table, not just you. PokerTracker 4 only expects to see the hero's hole cards — the extra lines confuse the parser and can cause it to misread the rest of the hand.

**Timezone and stray lines.** CoinPoker timestamps hands in CEST (or whatever server timezone it's running), and adds lines like `Hand was run once` and `Game ended:` that don't exist in the format PokerTracker 4 reads.

None of this is a bug in CoinPoker's export — it's just a different dialect. The fix is a straight text conversion, not a workaround inside PokerTracker 4 itself.

## Converting your hand histories

1. Export your hand history file from CoinPoker as you normally would (`.txt`).
2. Upload it to [PokerHandsConverter](/) — cash games and full sessions both work, and tournament hands are detected automatically.
3. Download the converted file and point PokerTracker 4's importer at it, the same way you'd import any other tracker-ready file.

The header, currency, "Dealt to" lines and timestamps are all rewritten in the process, so the file PokerTracker 4 sees is one it already knows how to read.

## After you import

Two things are worth checking once a session is in:

- If PokerTracker 4 throws a pot-size or rake error on a handful of hands, see [Fixing "Invalid Pot Size" errors on CoinPoker imports](/blog/fix-invalid-pot-size-error-coinpoker-import) — it's almost always one specific summary-line format.
- If your session times or daily stats look shifted by a few hours, that's a timezone setting, not a bug — [CoinPoker timezone settings for accurate stats](/blog/coinpoker-timezone-settings-tracking-stats) covers the three options.

Once hands are importing cleanly, the next step is usually [setting up your first HUD](/blog/setup-hud-coinpoker-pokertracker-4) so the stats actually show up at the table. If you play tournaments as well as cash, [tracking CoinPoker tournament results](/blog/track-coinpoker-tournament-results) is worth a read too — tournament hands are handled differently from cash hands under the hood.

## Which trackers does this work with?

The same conversion feeds PokerTracker 4, Hold'em Manager 3, Hand2Note and DriveHUD — see the [PokerTracker 4 vs Hold'em Manager 3](/blog/pokertracker-4-vs-holdem-manager-3-coinpoker) comparison if you haven't picked one yet, or the dedicated [Hold'em Manager 3 import guide](/blog/import-coinpoker-hands-into-holdem-manager-3) and [Hand2Note setup guide](/blog/hand2note-coinpoker-setup-guide) if you already have.

title: CoinPoker vs PokerStars Hand History Format: What's Different
excerpt: A field-by-field breakdown of why CoinPoker's hand history export isn't compatible with PokerStars-style trackers out of the box.
body:
## Two formats that look alike and aren't

If you've only ever played on PokerStars-descended sites, a CoinPoker hand history reads as *almost* familiar — same general shape, same idea of seats and streets and a summary line. The specific fields are different enough that a tracker built for PokerStars-style imports (which is most of them) rejects CoinPoker's export outright, or worse, imports it with wrong numbers.

## Field-by-field differences

**Hand header.** PokerStars-style: `PokerStars Hand #123: Hold'em No Limit ($0.01/$0.02 USD) - 2026/09/09 12:01:21 ET`. CoinPoker: `CoinPoker Hand #130114200045: NLH (₮0.01/₮0.02) 2026/09/09 12:01:21 CEST`. Different hand-id prefix, an abbreviated game code (`NLH` instead of the full name), and the tether sign instead of a dollar sign with a currency code.

**Currency.** CoinPoker denominates cash games in USDT and prints the ₮ symbol throughout — blinds, bets, the summary, everywhere an amount appears. Trackers expecting `$` (or an explicit `USD` code) don't recognize ₮ as a currency at all, so every amount in the hand looks unparseable.

**Hole cards.** CoinPoker's export includes a `Dealt to <name>` line for every player at the table, since the client itself has visibility CoinPoker chooses to log. Trackers expect exactly one `Dealt to` line — yours — and can misparse the hand when they hit extra ones for opponents.

**Timezone.** CoinPoker stamps hands in the server's local time (commonly CEST), with no explicit "ET" marker. Trackers built around PokerStars conventions generally expect either a bare local timestamp or an explicit Eastern-time stamp, depending on how you configure them — see [timezone settings for accurate stats](/blog/coinpoker-timezone-settings-tracking-stats) for the tradeoffs.

**Fee lines.** Some CoinPoker cash tables add a `Splash Fee` on top of rake in the summary line — a fee type PokerStars-style parsers have no concept of. Left as-is, it breaks rake parsing on the hand entirely; see [CoinPoker rake and Splash Fee explained](/blog/coinpoker-rake-splash-fee-explained) for exactly how.

**Extra bookkeeping lines.** `Hand was run once`, `Game ended:` and similar lines are informational text CoinPoker adds that don't correspond to anything in the PokerStars-style format, and get treated as noise.

## Why this matters beyond "it won't import"

Even when a tracker *does* manage to import a raw CoinPoker file, misreading the currency sign or an extra "Dealt to" line can silently produce wrong pot sizes, wrong win-rates, or a HUD that shows stats for the wrong player. A hand that imports without an error isn't the same as a hand that imported *correctly*.

## The practical fix

Rather than trying to reconfigure a tracker's parser (most don't expose that), convert the file first: [see the full CoinPoker → PokerTracker 4 walkthrough](/blog/import-coinpoker-hands-into-pokertracker-4). The same conversion works whether you're headed to PokerTracker 4, Hold'em Manager 3 or Hand2Note.

title: PokerTracker 4 vs Hold'em Manager 3 for CoinPoker: Which Should You Use?
excerpt: Both trackers work fine with CoinPoker hands once converted — here's what actually differs between them so you can pick one.
body:
## Same job, different tools

PokerTracker 4 and Hold'em Manager 3 both do the same core job — import hand histories, compute stats, and feed a HUD at the table — and both work fine with CoinPoker hands once they're converted to a format either one recognizes. The choice between them mostly comes down to interface preference and which one your study group or coaching material already uses, not raw capability.

## PokerTracker 4

PokerTracker 4 has been around the longest of the two, and it shows in the depth of its filtering and reporting — if you like slicing your database by very specific situations (3-bet pots from the blinds, specific stack-depth ranges, and so on), PT4's report builder is built for exactly that. The HUD is fully customizable panel by panel, which is powerful but has a steeper setup curve the first time — see [setting up your first HUD in PokerTracker 4](/blog/setup-hud-coinpoker-pokertracker-4) if you're starting from scratch.

## Hold'em Manager 3

Hold'em Manager 3 leans more modern in its interface, with a replayer and stats views that are generally considered a bit more approachable out of the box. It covers the same core stat set as PT4 and is a common choice for players who want less configuration before they can start reviewing sessions. See the [CoinPoker → Hold'em Manager 3 import guide](/blog/import-coinpoker-hands-into-holdem-manager-3) for the exact steps.

## What actually matters for CoinPoker players specifically

Neither tracker understands CoinPoker's raw export — the ₮ currency sign, the abbreviated `NLH` header, and the extra `Dealt to` lines trip up both parsers the same way. [PokerHandsConverter](/) converts to a format both trackers read correctly, so the choice between PT4 and HM3 doesn't depend on which one "supports" CoinPoker — they both do, once the file is converted.

## If you're not sure yet

A reasonable default: if you already use one for other sites, keep using it — switching trackers mid-database is more friction than it's worth for most players. If you're starting from zero, try the free/trial version of each on a small batch of converted hands and see which interface you reach for without thinking. Both read cash games and tournaments correctly once converted; see [tracking CoinPoker tournament results](/blog/track-coinpoker-tournament-results) either way, since tournament hands have their own quirks regardless of which tracker reads them.

title: How to Set Up Your First HUD for CoinPoker in PokerTracker 4
excerpt: A HUD only shows what's in your database. Here's how to get from zero hands imported to a working, readable HUD at the table.
body:
## Why the HUD doesn't "just appear"

A HUD (heads-up display) overlays live stats — VPIP, PFR, 3-bet%, and whatever else you configure — directly on the table while you play. It's driven entirely by hands already sitting in your tracker's database, so if it isn't showing anything, the usual cause is one of two things: no hands have been imported yet, or the HUD hasn't been pointed at the right site/table type.

## Before you touch HUD settings

Make sure your CoinPoker hands are actually importing first. If PokerTracker 4 is throwing errors on import, the HUD has nothing to draw from — see [importing CoinPoker hands into PokerTracker 4](/blog/import-coinpoker-hands-into-pokertracker-4) and, if a subset of hands specifically error out, [fixing "Invalid Pot Size" errors](/blog/fix-invalid-pot-size-error-coinpoker-import).

## Setting up a basic HUD

1. **Import a session first.** You need at least a few dozen hands in the database before stats are meaningful — a brand-new HUD showing "0 hands" everywhere isn't broken, it just has nothing to show yet.
2. **Pick a HUD profile.** PokerTracker 4 ships default profiles (a simple one, a more detailed one) — start with a simple profile rather than building a custom panel layout from scratch on day one.
3. **Choose your stat panels.** The standard starting set most players settle on is VPIP, PFR, 3-bet%, and a hand count (so you know how much to trust the numbers yet) — that's usually enough to be useful without cluttering the table.
4. **Match it to the table.** HUD profiles can be table-size specific (6-max vs full ring) and game-type specific (cash vs tournament) — a HUD tuned for 6-max cash won't necessarily make sense pulled into a tournament, since population tendencies and sample sizes are completely different there. See [tracking CoinPoker tournament results](/blog/track-coinpoker-tournament-results) for what's different about tournament stats specifically.
5. **Sit down and confirm it's live.** Open a table (or the replayer) and check the panel renders and updates — small sample sizes will make the numbers jump around a lot at first, which is expected, not a sign anything's wrong.

## Reading small samples correctly

Early on, a HUD stat built on 20 hands can look extreme — a 45% VPIP that means almost nothing yet. Most players configure a minimum hand-count threshold before trusting a stat, or watch the hand-count number next to each stat rather than the stat alone until the sample builds up.

## Once it's working

If you switch between PokerTracker 4 and Hold'em Manager 3, or haven't picked yet, the HUD setup differs in interface but not in the underlying idea — see [PokerTracker 4 vs Hold'em Manager 3 for CoinPoker](/blog/pokertracker-4-vs-holdem-manager-3-coinpoker) for how they compare.

title: Fixing "Invalid Pot Size" Errors When Importing CoinPoker Hands
excerpt: Almost every 'Invalid Pot Size' error on a CoinPoker import traces back to one specific summary-line format. Here's how to fix it.
body:
## The single most common CoinPoker import error

If PokerTracker 4 rejects a CoinPoker hand with something like *"Invalid pot size"* — and it's happening on a large share of your hands, not just one or two — there's a specific, well-understood cause: a newer CoinPoker summary-line format that includes a **Splash Fee** alongside the rake.

## What's actually in the file

A normal CoinPoker summary line looks like:

```
Total pot ₮3.67 | Rake ₮0.18
```

Some cash tables now add a Splash Fee on top:

```
Total pot ₮3.67 | Rake ₮0.18 | Splash Fee ₮0.02
```

PokerTracker 4 has no concept of a "Splash Fee" — and its presence in the line doesn't just get ignored, it stops PT4 from reading the `Rake` figure at all. PT4 then computes rake as `0`, checks that against the pot it calculated independently from the betting action, finds a mismatch, and rejects the hand as an invalid pot.

## Why it looks stake-specific (but isn't)

Because the Splash Fee shows up more often on certain tables, this can look like a stakes-specific bug at first — "my NL10 hands are fine but NL2 keeps failing." It isn't tied to a stake; it's tied to whichever tables happen to charge that fee. The fix has to apply uniformly, regardless of stake, or you'll just see the same failure resurface on a different table later. See [CoinPoker rake and Splash Fee explained](/blog/coinpoker-rake-splash-fee-explained) for how the fee affects your tracked stats beyond just this import error.

## The fix

[PokerHandsConverter](/) detects the Splash Fee pattern and folds it into the rake figure PokerTracker 4 already understands, so the line above becomes:

```
Total pot $3.67 | Rake $0.20
```

That's the rake PT4's own independent calculation expects — pot equals collected amounts plus rake, balanced, no mismatch, no rejected hand. If you're seeing this error on a file today, re-running it through the converter resolves it without touching anything in PokerTracker 4 itself.

## If you're still seeing pot-size errors after converting

A few other things produce a similar-looking error and are worth ruling out:

- **Run-it-twice boards.** These get flagged as warnings during conversion rather than guessed at silently — check your conversion history for a warning on the specific hand.
- **A genuinely corrupted export.** Rare, but if CoinPoker's own export was truncated mid-file, no converter can reconstruct the missing data.

For the broader list of formatting differences between CoinPoker and PokerStars-style hands (of which Splash Fee is one), see [CoinPoker vs PokerStars hand history format](/blog/coinpoker-vs-pokerstars-hand-history-format).

meta_description: Why PokerTracker 4 rejects CoinPoker hands with an "Invalid Pot Size" error, and how the Splash Fee summary line format causes it.

title: How to Import CoinPoker Hands into Hold'em Manager 3
excerpt: A raw CoinPoker export won't import cleanly into Hold'em Manager 3 either — here's the fix, plus what to check afterward.
body:
## Hold'em Manager 3 and CoinPoker's raw export

Like PokerTracker 4, Hold'em Manager 3 is built around a PokerStars-style hand history format. CoinPoker's raw export — the ₮ currency sign, the abbreviated `NLH` header, a `Dealt to` line for every player, and the local-timezone timestamp — isn't something HM3's importer recognizes out of the box, so a raw file typically fails to import or imports with distorted numbers.

## Converting first

1. Export your hand history from CoinPoker (`.txt`).
2. Run it through [PokerHandsConverter](/) — the header, currency, hole-card lines and timestamp all get rewritten into the format Hold'em Manager 3 expects.
3. Import the converted file into Hold'em Manager 3 through its normal file-import flow, the same way you'd import from any other supported site.

Cash hands come out with dollar amounts attached; tournament hands keep bare chip counts, since that's the format a tournament hand is supposed to be in — see [tracking CoinPoker tournament results](/blog/track-coinpoker-tournament-results) if tournaments are most of your volume.

## What to check after importing

A small number of hands failing to import, specifically with a pot or rake mismatch, is almost always one specific cause — see [fixing "Invalid Pot Size" errors](/blog/fix-invalid-pot-size-error-coinpoker-import). It applies the same way regardless of which tracker you're importing into.

If your session stats look shifted by a few hours from when you actually played, that's a timezone display setting, not a data problem — [CoinPoker timezone settings for accurate stats](/blog/coinpoker-timezone-settings-tracking-stats) walks through the three options.

## HUD setup

Once hands are in, Hold'em Manager 3's HUD works from the same idea as PokerTracker 4's — pick a profile, choose your stat panels, match it to cash vs tournament — just with a different settings interface. If you're deciding between the two trackers rather than committed to HM3 already, [PokerTracker 4 vs Hold'em Manager 3 for CoinPoker](/blog/pokertracker-4-vs-holdem-manager-3-coinpoker) covers what actually differs between them for a CoinPoker player specifically.

title: Using Hand2Note with CoinPoker Hand Histories: Setup Guide
excerpt: Hand2Note expects PokerStars-style hands, same as PT4 and HM3. Here's how to get CoinPoker hand histories into it correctly.
body:
## Where Hand2Note fits

Hand2Note is built around fast, visual range and population analysis — heatmaps, range charts, and a HUD that leans on that same visual approach. Like PokerTracker 4 and Hold'em Manager 3, it expects a PokerStars-style hand history, so a raw CoinPoker export runs into the same header, currency and timestamp mismatches described in [CoinPoker vs PokerStars hand history format](/blog/coinpoker-vs-pokerstars-hand-history-format).

## Getting CoinPoker hands into Hand2Note

1. Export your hands from CoinPoker as usual.
2. Convert the file with [PokerHandsConverter](/) — this handles the header rewrite, the ₮-to-$ currency conversion, and stripping the extra `Dealt to` lines CoinPoker adds for every player at the table.
3. Import the converted file into Hand2Note through its standard hand history import.

Both cash and tournament hands are detected and converted correctly — cash hands get real dollar amounts, tournament hands keep chip counts, matching what Hand2Note expects for each format. See [tracking CoinPoker tournament results](/blog/track-coinpoker-tournament-results) for what's specifically different about how tournament hands get tracked.

## A note on timezone

Hand2Note's session and daily views are sensitive to accurate timestamps, same as any tracker. CoinPoker logs hands in local server time (often CEST) with no timezone marker — if your session breakdowns look off by a few hours, it's a timestamp formatting choice, not missing data. [CoinPoker timezone settings for accurate stats](/blog/coinpoker-timezone-settings-tracking-stats) covers the three ways to handle it during conversion.

## Troubleshooting a failed import

If a batch of hands specifically fails with a pot or rake mismatch rather than a generic format error, that's very likely the Splash Fee issue described in [fixing "Invalid Pot Size" errors](/blog/fix-invalid-pot-size-error-coinpoker-import) — it affects every PokerStars-style tracker the same way, Hand2Note included, and the fix is the same: re-convert the file.

## Comparing trackers

If you haven't settled on Hand2Note specifically and are weighing it against PokerTracker 4 or Hold'em Manager 3, see [PokerTracker 4 vs Hold'em Manager 3 for CoinPoker](/blog/pokertracker-4-vs-holdem-manager-3-coinpoker) — the core tradeoffs (report depth vs a more visual, range-first workflow) carry over to Hand2Note as a third option.

title: CoinPoker Timezone Settings: Getting Accurate Session and Daily Stats
excerpt: A timezone mismatch can make a real session look split in two, or shift your 'today' by several hours. Here are the three ways to handle it.
body:
## Why timezone trips people up

CoinPoker timestamps hands in the server's local time — commonly CEST — with no explicit timezone marker in the hand header. Trackers built around PokerStars-style imports generally expect either a plain local timestamp or an explicit Eastern-time stamp appended in brackets, depending on how the tracker's session and daily-stats views are configured. Get this mismatched and your "today" in the tracker can quietly include hands from what felt like yesterday's session, or split one real session into two.

## The three options

When converting a CoinPoker file, you choose per upload:

**Keep local time and add an `[… ET]` stamp (the default).** The hand keeps its original local timestamp, with an Eastern-time equivalent appended in brackets — this is the closest match to what most PokerStars-style trackers expect out of the box, and it's a safe default if you're not sure which your tracker wants.

**Output a single Eastern-time stamp.** The hand's timestamp is converted outright to Eastern time rather than kept local-plus-annotated. Useful if your tracker's session/daily views are explicitly configured around Eastern time and you don't want the dual-stamp format.

**Leave CoinPoker's time untouched.** No conversion at all — useful mainly for debugging, or if you're feeding the file into something else entirely that doesn't expect either of the above.

Nothing changes without you picking one; there's no silent default that surprises you later.

## Which one should you actually use?

For most players running PokerTracker 4, Hold'em Manager 3 or Hand2Note out of the box, the default (`[… ET]` stamp) is the right call — it's what those trackers are generally set up to parse. If your session-length or daily-volume stats look wrong after importing, check this setting before assuming the hand data itself is bad; a timezone mismatch produces exactly that symptom — sessions that look too short, too long, or split oddly — without any hand actually being corrupted.

## This matters more for tournaments

Tournament session boundaries (registration close, late-reg windows, overall session length across a multi-table tournament) are more sensitive to timestamp accuracy than a single cash session is. See [tracking CoinPoker tournament results](/blog/track-coinpoker-tournament-results) if tournaments are a meaningful share of your volume.

## Related formatting differences

Timezone is one of several places CoinPoker's export differs from the PokerStars-style format trackers expect — see the full rundown in [CoinPoker vs PokerStars hand history format](/blog/coinpoker-vs-pokerstars-hand-history-format), or start from [importing CoinPoker hands into PokerTracker 4](/blog/import-coinpoker-hands-into-pokertracker-4) if you haven't converted a file yet.

title: How to Track CoinPoker Tournament Results in Your HUD Software
excerpt: Tournament hands aren't cash hands with chips instead of dollars — here's what's actually different about tracking them correctly.
body:
## Tournaments aren't just "cash games with chips"

Trackers treat tournament hands differently from cash hands at a structural level, and that starts with the hand history itself. CoinPoker tournament hands keep bare chip counts rather than dollar amounts — correctly so, since blinds and stacks change level to level and don't map to a fixed dollar value the way a cash table's do. A converter (or a tracker) that tried to attach dollar signs to tournament chip counts would be actively wrong, not just unhelpful.

[PokerHandsConverter](/) detects the format per hand automatically — cash hands get proper dollar amounts, tournament hands keep chip counts — so a mixed session file with both cash and tournament hands in it converts correctly without you having to split anything by hand first.

## What to check once tournament hands are imported

**Buy-in and fee tracking.** Make sure your tracker's ROI and profit views are reading buy-in and fee correctly for CoinPoker's specific tournament fee structure — this is where most tournament-tracking confusion actually comes from, not the hand data itself.

**Blind-level context.** Because stacks are relative to a moving blind level, stats like "stack depth" or "M-ratio" only mean something in the context of the current level — this is inherent to tournament tracking generally, not specific to CoinPoker, but worth knowing before you read too much into a single hand's numbers.

**Session boundaries.** Multi-table tournaments can run for hours across a single logical "session" in your tracker. If your timestamps are off — see [CoinPoker timezone settings for accurate stats](/blog/coinpoker-timezone-settings-tracking-stats) — a long tournament can appear to be split into disconnected pieces in your daily view.

## HUD considerations for tournaments

A HUD profile tuned for 6-max cash doesn't carry over cleanly to tournaments — population tendencies shift enormously as stacks get shallower and antes kick in, and a cash-tuned HUD will often show you stats calculated over too few relevant hands to mean anything at a given stack depth. If you're setting up a HUD for the first time, [setting up your first HUD in PokerTracker 4](/blog/setup-hud-coinpoker-pokertracker-4) covers the basics, including matching a profile to the right game type.

## Getting started

If you haven't converted a tournament file yet, the process is identical to cash: export from CoinPoker, convert, import. See [importing CoinPoker hands into PokerTracker 4](/blog/import-coinpoker-hands-into-pokertracker-4) for the full walkthrough, or the [Hold'em Manager 3](/blog/import-coinpoker-hands-into-holdem-manager-3) and [Hand2Note](/blog/hand2note-coinpoker-setup-guide) guides if you're on a different tracker.

title: CoinPoker Rake and Splash Fee Explained: How They Affect Your Tracked Stats
excerpt: A newer CoinPoker fee type breaks rake parsing in every major tracker if left unconverted. Here's what it is and how it's handled.
body:
## Rake is old news. Splash Fee is newer, and less understood.

Every poker site takes rake — that part isn't CoinPoker-specific. What trips people up is a newer line item some CoinPoker cash tables add on top of rake: a **Splash Fee**. It's a separate charge, printed separately in the hand summary, and — critically — most PokerStars-style trackers have no idea what to do with it.

## How it shows up in the hand history

A standard summary line:

```
Total pot ₮3.67 | Rake ₮0.18
```

With a Splash Fee added:

```
Total pot ₮3.67 | Rake ₮0.18 | Splash Fee ₮0.02
```

The pot total already accounts for both the rake and the Splash Fee — CoinPoker isn't hiding anything, it's just reporting two separate deductions instead of one.

## Why it breaks tracker imports

PokerTracker 4, Hold'em Manager 3 and Hand2Note are all built to expect a summary line that ends after the rake figure. When a Splash Fee is appended, the tracker's parser doesn't recognize the trailing text — and rather than ignoring it gracefully, it typically stops reading the rake figure at all, computes rake as `0`, and then rejects the hand because the pot it calculates from the betting action doesn't match the (now wrong) rake-adjusted total. See [fixing "Invalid Pot Size" errors](/blog/fix-invalid-pot-size-error-coinpoker-import) for the exact mechanics.

## How it affects your tracked stats if left unconverted

Beyond the outright import failures, a Splash Fee that isn't accounted for correctly can distort:

- **Total rake paid** — understated, since the tracker never saw the fee at all.
- **Big-blinds-won-per-100** and similar rate stats — thrown off on any hand where the pot mismatch caused the whole hand to be skipped rather than just misread.
- **Session profit** — skipped hands simply don't count toward the session, which can make a losing session look smaller (or a winning one look bigger) than it actually was.

## The fix

[PokerHandsConverter](/) folds the Splash Fee into the rake figure automatically during conversion, so the tracker sees one number it already understands — `Rake $0.20` instead of `Rake $0.18 | Splash Fee $0.02` — and the pot balances correctly. This applies uniformly across every stake, since the fee isn't tied to any one table type.

## Related reading

For the rest of the formatting gap between CoinPoker and PokerStars-style hand histories — currency signs, headers, timezone — see [CoinPoker vs PokerStars hand history format](/blog/coinpoker-vs-pokerstars-hand-history-format), or start from [importing CoinPoker hands into PokerTracker 4](/blog/import-coinpoker-hands-into-pokertracker-4) if you're converting your first file.
